admissions as laid , down in those rules. It appears that 
the proportion fixed in the old Communal G. 0. has 
been adhered to even after the commencement of the 
Constitution on January 26, 1950. Indeed, G. 0. 
No. 2208, dated June 16, 1950, laying down rules for 
the selection of candidates for admission into the 
Medical Colleges substantially repi;oduces the communal 
proportion fixed in the old Commu111l G. 0. 
On June 7, 1950, Srimathi Champakam Dorairajan 
made an application to the High Court of Judicature 
at Madras under article 226 of the Constitution for 
protection of her fundamental rights under article 15 
(1) and article 29 (2) of the Consiitution and prayed 
for the issue of a writ of mandamus or other suitable 
prerogative writ restraining the State of Madras and 
all officers and subordinates thereof from enforcing, 
observing, maintaining or following or requiring the 
enforcement, observance, maintenance 9r following by 
the authorities concerned of the notification or order 
generally referred to as the Communal G. 0. in and by 
which admissions into the Madras Medical Colleges 
were sought or purported to be regulated in such 
manner as to infringe and involve the violation of her 
fundamental rights. From the affidavit filed in sup­
port of her petition, it does not appear that the 
petitioner had actually applied for admission in the 
Medical College. She states that on inquiry she came 
to know that she would not be admitted to the College 
as she belonged to the Brahmin community. No 
objection, however, was taken to the maintainability 
of her petition on the ground of absence of any actual 
application for admission made by her. On the con­
trary, we have been told that the State had agreed 
to reserve a seat for her, should her application before f 
the High Court succeed. In the peculiar circumstances, 
we do not consider it necessary to pursue this matter 
any further. But we desire to guard ourselves against , 
being understood as holding that we approve of a 
person who has not actually applied for admission 
into an cduca;ional institution coming to Court com­
plaining of infringement of any fundamental right

[Page 5]
S.C.R. SUPREME COURT REPORTS 529 
under article 29 (2). The High Court by its judgment 
delivered on July ll, 1950, allowed this application of 
Srimathi Champakam Dorairajan. The State ,of 
Madras has now come up before us on appeal which has 
been numbered Case No. 270 of 1951. 
Sri Srinivasan who had actually applied for admis­
sion into the Government Engineering College at 
Guindy, filed a petition praying for a writ of mandamus 
or any other writ restraining the State of Madras .and 
all officers thereof from enforcing, observing, maintain­
ing or following the Communal G.O. in and by which 
admission into the Engineering College was sought to 
be regulated in such manner as to infringe and 
involve the violation of the fundamental right of the 
petitioner under article 15 (1) and artide 29 (2) of the 
Constitution. In the affidavit filed in support of his 
petition, the petitioner has stated that he had passed 
the Intermediate Examination held in March, 1950, in 
Group 1, passing the said examination in the first class 
and obtaining marks set out in paragraph 1 of his 
affidavit. It will appear that in the optionals which 
are taken into consideration in determining the 
academic test for admission in the Engineering College 
the petitioner Srinivasan secured 369 marks out of a 
maximum of 450 marks. The High Court has by the 
same judgment allowed this application also and the 
State has filed an appeal which has been numbered 
271 of 1951. The learned counsel appearing for the 
State of Madras conceded that these two applicants 
would have been admitted to the educational institu­
tions they intended to join and they. would not have 
been denied admission if selections had been made on 
merits alone. 
Article 29 which occurs in Part III of the Constitu­
tion under the head "Cultural and Educational Rights" 
runs as follows : 
"(1) Any section of the citizens residing in the 
territory of India or any part thereof having a distinct 
language, script or culture of its own shall have the 
right to conserve the same.

(2) No citizen shall be denied admission into any 
educational institution maintained by the State or 
receiving aid out of State funds on grounds only of 
religion, race, caste, language or any of them. 
It will be noticed that while clause ( 1) protects the 
language, script or culture of a section of the citizens, 
clause (2) guarantees the fundamental right of an indivi­
dual citizen. The right to get admission into any 
educational institution of the kind mentioned in clause 
(2) •is a right which an indivjdual citizen has as a 
citizen and not as a member of any community or class 
of citizens. This right is not to be denied to the citizen 
on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or 
any of them. If a citizen who seeks admission into 
any such educational institution has not the requisite 
academic qualifications and is 'denied admission on 
that ground, he certainly cannot be heard to complain 
of an infraction of his fundamental right under this 
article. But, on the other hand, if he has the academic 
qualifications but is refused admission on! y on grounds 
of religion, race, caste, language or any of them, then 
there is a clear breaclt of his fundamental right. 
The learned Advocate-General appearing for the 
State contends that the provisions of this article have 
to be read along with other articles in the Constitu­
tion. He urges that article "6 charges the State with 
promoting with special care the educational and 
economic interests of the weaker sections of the people, 
and, in particular, of the Scheduled Castes and the 
Scheduled Tribes, and with protecting them from social 
injustice and all forms of exploitation. It is pointed 
out that although this article finds a place in Part IV 
of the Constitution which lays down certain directive 
principles of State policy and though the provisions 
contained in that Part are not enforceable by any 
Court, the principles therein laid down are nevertheless 
fundamental for the governance of the country and 
article 37 makes it obligatory on the part of the State 
to apply those principles in making laws. The argu· 
ment is that having regard to the provisions of article 
"6, the State is entitled to maintain the Communal

[Page 7]
S.C.R. SUPREME COURT REPORTS 531 
G. 0. fixing proportionate seats for different commu­
nities and if because of that Order, which is thus con­
tended to be valid in law and not in violation of the 
Constitution, the petitioners are unable to get admis­
sions into the educational institutions, there is no 
infringement of their fundamental rights. · Indeed, the 
learned Advocate-General of ·Madras even contends 
that the provisions of article 46 override the provisions 
of article 29(2). We reject the above noted contentions 
completely. The directive principles of the State policy, 
which by article 37 are expressly made unenforceable 
by a Court, cannot -override the provisions found in 
Part III which, notwithstanding other provisions, are 
expressly made enforceable by appropriate Writs, 
Orders or directions under article 32. The chapter of 
Fundamental Rights is sacrosanct and not liable to be 
abridged by any Legislative or Executive Act or 
order, except to the extent provided in the appropriate 
article in Part III. The directive principles of State 
policy have to conform to and run as subsidiary to the 
Chapter of Fundamental Rights. In our opinion, that 
is the correct way in which the provisions found in 
Parts III and IV have to be understood. However, so 
long as there is no infringement of any Fundamental 
Right, to the extent conferred by the provisions in 
Part III, there can be no objection to the State acting 
in accordance with the directive principles set out in 
Part IV, but subject again to the Legislative and 
Executive powers and limitations . conferred on the 
State under different provisions of the Constitution. 
In the next place, it will be noticed that article 16 
which guarantees the fundamental right of equality of 
opportunity in matters of public employment and pro­
vides that .no citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, 
race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or 
any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against 
in respect of any employment or office under the State 
also_ includes a specific clause iii the following terms :-
" ( 4) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State 
from ma!cing any provision for the reservation of 
appointments of posts in favour of any backward class

If the arguments founded on article 416 were sound 
then clause ( 4) of article 16 would have been wholly 
unnecessary and redundant. Seeing, however, that clause 
( 4) was inserted in artick 16, the omission of such an 
express provision from article 29 cannot but be re­
garded as significant. It may well be that the intention 
of the Constitution was not to introduce at all com­
munal considerations in matters _of admission into any 
educational institution maintained by the State or 
receiving aid out of State funds. The protection of 
backward classes of citizens may require appointment 
of members of backward classes in State services and 
the reason why power has been given to the State to 
provide for reservation of such appointments for back­
ward classes. may under those circumstances be under­
stood, That consideration, however, was not obviously 
considered pccessary in the case of admission into an 
educational institution and that may well be the reason 
for the omission from article 29 of a clause similar to 
clause ( 4) of article 16. 
Take the case of the petitioner Srinivasan. It is not 
disputed that he secured a much larger number of 
marks than the marks secured by many of the Non­
Brahmin candidates and yet the Non-Brahmin can­
didates who secured less number of marks will be 
admitted into six out of every 14 seats but the petitioner 
Srinivasan will not be admitted into any of them. 
What is the reason for this denial of admission except 
that he is a Brahmin and not a Non-Brahmin. He may 
have secured higher marks than the Anglo-Indian and 
Indian Christians or Muslim candidates but, never­
theless, he cannot get any of the scats reserved for the 
last mentioned communities for no fault of his except 
that he is a Brahmin and not a member of the afore­
said communities. Such denial of admission cannot 
but be regarded as made on ground only of his caste. 
It is argued that the petitioners arc ·not denied 
admission only because they arc Brahmins but for a

[Page 9]
S.C.R. SUPREME COURT REPORTS 533 
variety of reasons, e.g., (a) they are Brahmins, (ho) 
8rahmins have an allotment of only · two scats out of 
l4 and ( c) the two scats have already been filled up 
by more meritorious Brahmin candidates. This may 
be true so far as these two seats reserved for the 
· 8rahmins arc concerned but this line of argument can 
have no force when we come to consider .the scats 
reserved for candidates of other communities, for, so 
far as those seats are concerned, the petitioners are 
denied admission into any of them not on any ground 
other than the sole ground of their being Brahmins 
and not being members of the community for whom 
those reservations have been made. The classification 
in the Communal G. 0. proceeds on the basis of reli­
gion, race and caste. In our view, the classification 
made in the Communal G. 0. is opposed to the Consti­
tution and constitutes a clear violation of the funda­
mental rights guaranteed to the citizen under article 
29 (2). In this view of the matter, we do not find it 
necessary to consider the effect of articles 14 or 15 on 
the specific articles discussed above. 
For the reasons stated above, we arc of opinion that 
the Communal G. 0. being inconsistent with the pro­
visions of article 29 (2) in Part III of the Constitution 
is void under article 13. The result, therefore, is that 
these appeals stand dismissed with costs. 
Appeals dismissed.

under article 29 (2). The High Court by its judgment

Article 29 which occurs in Part III of the Constitu­
tion under the head "Cultural and Educational Rights" 
runs as follows : 
"(1) Any section of the citizens residing in the 
territory of India or any part thereof having a distinct

It will be noticed that while clause ( 1) protects the 
language, script or culture of a section of the citizens, 
clause (2) guarantees the fundamental right of an indivi­
dual citizen. The right to get admission into any 
educational institution of the kind mentioned in clause 
(2) •is a right which an indivjdual citizen has as a 
citizen and not as a member of any community or class 
of citizens. This right is not to be denied to the citizen 
on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or 
any of them. If a citizen who seeks admission into 
any such educational institution has not the requisite 
academic qualifications and is 'denied admission on 
that ground, he certainly cannot be heard to complain 
of an infraction of his fundamental right under this 
article. But, on the other hand, if he has the academic 
qualifications but is refused admission on! y on grounds 
of religion, race, caste, language or any of them, then 
there is a clear breaclt of his fundamental right. 
The learned Advocate-General appearing for the 
State contends that the provisions of this article have 
to be read along with other articles in the Constitu­
tion. He urges that article "6 charges the State with 
promoting with special care the educational and 
economic interests of the weaker sections of the people, 
and, in particular, of the Scheduled Castes and the 
Scheduled Tribes, and with protecting them from social 
injustice and all forms of exploitation. It is pointed 
out that although this article finds a place in Part IV 
of the Constitution which lays down certain directive 
principles of State policy and though the provisions 
contained in that Part are not enforceable by any 
Court, the principles therein laid down are nevertheless 
fundamental for the governance of the country and 
article 37 makes it obligatory on the part of the State 
to apply those principles in making laws. The argu· 
ment is that having regard to the provisions of article 
"6, the State is entitled to maintain the Communal

infringement of their fundamental rights. · Indeed, the 
learned Advocate-General of ·Madras even contends 
that the provisions of article 46 override the provisions 
of article 29(2). We reject the above noted contentions 
completely. The directive principles of the State policy, 
which by article 37 are expressly made unenforceable 
by a Court, cannot -override the provisions found in 
Part III which, notwithstanding other provisions, are 
expressly made enforceable by appropriate Writs, 
Orders or directions under article 32. The chapter of 
Fundamental Rights is sacrosanct and not liable to be 
abridged by any Legislative or Executive Act or 
order, except to the extent provided in the appropriate 
article in Part III. The directive principles of State 
policy have to conform to and run as subsidiary to the 
Chapter of Fundamental Rights. In our opinion, that 
is the correct way in which the provisions found in 
Parts III and IV have to be understood. However, so 
long as there is no infringement of any Fundamental 
Right, to the extent conferred by the provisions in 
Part III, there can be no objection to the State acting 
in accordance with the directive principles set out in 
Part IV, but subject again to the Legislative and 
Executive powers and limitations . conferred on the 
State under different provisions of the Constitution. 
In the next place, it will be noticed that article 16 
which guarantees the fundamental right of equality of 
opportunity in matters of public employment and pro­

race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or 
any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against 
in respect of any employment or office under the State

If the arguments founded on article 416 were sound 
then clause ( 4) of article 16 would have been wholly 
unnecessary and redundant. Seeing, however, that clause 
( 4) was inserted in artick 16, the omission of such an 
express provision from article 29 cannot but be re­
garded as significant. It may well be that the intention 
of the Constitution was not to introduce at all com­
munal considerations in matters _of admission into any 
educational institution maintained by the State or 
receiving aid out of State funds. The protection of 
backward classes of citizens may require appointment 
of members of backward classes in State services and 
the reason why power has been given to the State to 
provide for reservation of such appointments for back­
ward classes. may under those circumstances be under­
stood, That consideration, however, was not obviously 
considered pccessary in the case of admission into an 
educational institution and that may well be the reason 
for the omission from article 29 of a clause similar to 
clause ( 4) of article 16. 
Take the case of the petitioner Srinivasan. It is not 
disputed that he secured a much larger number of 
marks than the marks secured by many of the Non­
Brahmin candidates and yet the Non-Brahmin can­
didates who secured less number of marks will be 
admitted into six out of every 14 seats but the petitioner 
Srinivasan will not be admitted into any of them. 
What is the reason for this denial of admission except 
that he is a Brahmin and not a Non-Brahmin. He may 
have secured higher marks than the Anglo-Indian and 
Indian Christians or Muslim candidates but, never­
theless, he cannot get any of the scats reserved for the 
last mentioned communities for no fault of his except 
that he is a Brahmin and not a member of the afore­
said communities. Such denial of admission cannot 
but be regarded as made on ground only of his caste. 
It is argued that the petitioners arc ·not denied 
admission only because they arc Brahmins but for a

variety of reasons, e.g., (a) they are Brahmins, (ho) 
8rahmins have an allotment of only · two scats out of 
l4 and ( c) the two scats have already been filled up 
by more meritorious Brahmin candidates. This may 
be true so far as these two seats reserved for the 
· 8rahmins arc concerned but this line of argument can 
have no force when we come to consider .the scats 
reserved for candidates of other communities, for, so 
far as those seats are concerned, the petitioners are 
denied admission into any of them not on any ground 
other than the sole ground of their being Brahmins 
and not being members of the community for whom 
those reservations have been made. The classification 
in the Communal G. 0. proceeds on the basis of reli­
gion, race and caste. In our view, the classification 
made in the Communal G. 0. is opposed to the Consti­
tution and constitutes a clear violation of the funda­
mental rights guaranteed to the citizen under article 
29 (2). In this view of the matter, we do not find it 
necessary to consider the effect of articles 14 or 15 on 
the specific articles discussed above. 
For the reasons stated above, we arc of opinion that 
the Communal G. 0. being inconsistent with the pro­
visions of article 29 (2) in Part III of the Constitution 
is void under article 13. The result, therefore, is that 
these appeals stand dismissed with costs. 
Appeals dismissed.

Since the enactment of the Government of India Act,

principles which govern the interpretation of the Legis­

ples is that none of the items in each List is to be read

is that where there is a seeming conflict between an 
entry in List II and an entry in List I, an attempt 
should be made to see whether the two entries cannot 
be reconciled so as to avoid a conflict of jurisdiction. 
This principle has been stressed in a number of cases 
by the Federal Court as well as by the Privy Council. 
In re The Central PrOtlinces and Berar Act No. XIV 
-0/ 1938(2), the question arose as to whether a tax on 
the sale of motor spirits was a tax on the sale of goods 
within entry 48 of the Provincial List or a duty of 
excise within entry 45 of the Federal list. Dealing 
with the difficulty which arose in that case, Gwyer C. J. 
observed as follows :-
"Only in the Indian Constitution Act can the parti­
cular problem arise which is now under consideration; 
and an endeavour must be made to solve it, as the 
Judicial Committee have said, by having recourse to 
the context and scheme of the Act, and a reconciliation 
attempted between two apparently conflicting jurisdic­
tions by reading the two entries together and by 
interpreting, and, where neceessary, 'modifying, the 
language of the one by that of the other. If indeed 
such a reconciliation should prove impossible, then, 
and only then, will the non-obstante clause operate and 
the federal power prevail; for the clause ought to be 
regarded as a last · resource, a witness to the imperfec­
tions of human expression and the fallibility of legal 
craftsmanship."

fully discussed in the case of Chiraniit Lal Chowdhury 
v. The Uhion of India and others('), and the principles 
laid down in that case may be summarized as follows : 
(1) The presumption is always in favour of the 
constitutionality of an enactment, since it must be 
assumed that the legislature understands and correctly 
appreciates the needs of its own people, that its laws 
are directed to problems ' made manifest by experience 
and its discriminations are based on adequate grollnds. 
(2) The presumption i;nay be rebutted in certain

is no classification ~t all and no difference peculiar to 
any individual or class and not applicable to any other 
individual or class, af\d yet the law hits only a parti­
cular individual or class. 
(3) The principle of equality does not mean that 
every law must have universal application for all i>er­
sons who are not by nature, attainment or circum­
stances in the same position, and the varying needs of 
different classes of persons often require separate 
treatment.

( 4) The principle does not take away from the State

produce some inequality, and mere production of 
inequality is not enough. 
(6) If a law de~ls equally with ~embers of a well­
defined class, it is not obnoxious and it is not open to 
the charge of denial of equal protection on the ground 
that it has no application to other persons. 
(7) While reasonable classification is permissible, 
such classification must be based upon some real and 
substantial distinction bearing a reasonable and just 
relation to the object sought to be attained, and the 
classification cannot be made arbitrarily and without 
any substantial basis. 
Similarly, Professor Willis, dealing with the Four­

"The guaranty of the equal protection of the laws 
means the protection of equal laws. It forbids class 
legislation, but does not forbid classification which 
rests upon reasonable grounds of distinction. It does 
not prohibit legislation, which is limited either in the 
objects to which it is directed or by the territory with­
in which it is to operate. 'It. merely requires that all 
persons subjected to such legislation shall be treated 
alike under like circumstances and conditions both iu 
the privileges conferred and in the liabilities imposed'. 
'The inhibition of the amendment .... was designed to 
prevent any person or class of persons from being 
singled out as a special subject for discriminating and 
hostile legislation.' It doc:; not take from the states

laws or tax laws, or eminent domain laws, but per­

and nullifies what they do only when it is without any 
reasonable ba,sis. Mathematical nicety and perfect 
equality are not required. Similarity, not identity of

Since the enactment of the Government of India Act, 
1935, there have been several cases in which the 
principles which govern the interpretation of the Legis­

in a narrow or restricted sense(1). The second principle 
is that where there is a seeming conflict between an 
entry in List II and an entry in List I, an attempt 
should be made to see whether the two entries cannot 
be reconciled so as to avoid a conflict of jurisdiction. 
This principle has been stressed in a number of cases 
by the Federal Court as well as by the Privy Council.

the sale of motor spirits was a tax on the sale of goods 
within entry 48 of the Provincial List or a duty of 
excise within entry 45 of the Federal list. Dealing 
with the difficulty which arose in that case, Gwyer C. J. 
observed as follows :-
"Only in the Indian Constitution Act can the parti­
cular problem arise which is now under consideration; 
and an endeavour must be made to solve it, as the

laid down in that case may be summarized as follows : 
(1) The presumption is always in favour of the 
constitutionality of an enactment, since it must be 
assumed that the legislature understands and correctly 
appreciates the needs of its own people, that its laws 
are directed to problems ' made manifest by experience 
and its discriminations are based on adequate grollnds.

any individual or class and not applicable to any other 
individual or class, af\d yet the law hits only a parti­

every law must have universal application for all i>er­

different classes of persons often require separate

(7) While reasonable classification is permissible, 
such classification must be based upon some real and

any substantial basis.

persons subjected to such legislation shall be treated

the privileges conferred and in the liabilities imposed'.

declared several important sections of the Act including

are in my view invalid cannot affect the validity of 
the Act as a whole. The test to be applied when an 
argument like the one addressed in this case is raised, 
has been very correctly summed up by the Privy 
Council in Attorney-General for Alberta v. Attorney-
General for Canada(1) in these words :-
"The real question is whether what remains is so 
inextricably bound up with the part declared invalid

as it has sometimes been put, whether on a fair review 
of the whole matter it can be assumed that the legis­

be invalid are not ~nextricably bound up with the

The Constitution (First Amendment) 'Act, 1951, which has 
inserted, inter alia, Arts. 31A and 31B in the Constitution of 
India is riot ultra vires or unconstitutional. 
The provisional Parliament is competent to exercise the power 
of amending the Constitution under Art. 368. The fact that the 
said article refers to the two Houses of the Parliament and the 
President separately and not to the Parliament, does not lead to 
the inference that the body which is invested with the power to 
amend is not the Parliament but a different body consisting of 
the two Houses. . 
The words "all the powers confer{ed by the provisions of this 
Constitution ori Parliament': in Art. 379 are not confined to such 
powers as could be exercised by · the provisional Parliament con-
sisting of a single chamber, but are wide enough to include the 
power to amend the Constitution conferred by Art. 368. 
The Constitution (Removal of Difficulties} Order No. 2 made 
by the President on the 26th January, 1950, which purports to 
adapt Art. 368 · by omitting "either House of" and "in each 
House" and substituting "Parliament" for "that House" is not

There is nothing in Art. 392 to suggest that the President should 
wait, before adapting a particular article, till the oc.casion 
actually arose for the provisional Parliament to exercise the 
power conferred by the article. 
The view that Art. 368 is a complete code in itself in respect 
of the procedure provided by it and does not contemplate any 
ainendment of a Bill for amendment of the Constitution after it 
has been introduced, and that if the Bill is amended during its 
passage through the House, the amendment Act cannot be said 
to have been passed in conformity with the procedure prescribed 
by Art. 368 and would be invalid, is erroneous. 
Although "Ia,v" must ordinarily include constitutional law 
there is a clear demarcation between ordinary law tvhich is made 
in the exercise of legislative power and constitutional law, 
which is made in the exercise of constituent power. In. the 
context of Art. 13, "law" must'be taken to mean rules or regula-
tions made in exercise of ordinary legislative po\ver and not 
amendments to the constitution made in the exercise of consti-
tuent power with the result that Art. 13(2) does not affect amend-
ments made under Art. 368. 
Articles 31A and 31B inserted in the Constitution by the 
Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, do not curtail the 
powers of the High Court under Art. 226 to issue writs for 
enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III or of the 
Supreme Court under Arts. 132 and 136 to entertain appeals 
from orders issuing or refusing such writs; but they only exclude 
from the purvie\v of Part III certain classes of cases. These 
articles therefore do not require ratification under cl. (b) of the 
proviso to Art. 368. 
Articles 3!A and 31B are not invalid on the ground that they 
relate to land \vhich is a matter covered by the State List (item 
18 of List II) as these articles are essentially amendments of the 
Constitution, and Parliament alone has the power to enact 
them.

Although "law" must ordinarily include constitu-
tional law, there is a clear demarcation between ordi-
nary law, which i~ made in exercise of legislative power, 
and constitutional law, which is made in exercise of 
constituent power. Dicey defines constitutional law as 
including "all rules which directly or indirectly affect 
the distribution or the exercise of the sovereign power 
in the State." It is thus mainly concerned with the 
creation of the three great organs of the State, the exe-
cutive, the legislature and the judiciary, the distribu-
tion of governmental power among them and the defi-
nition of their mutual relation. No doubt our constitu-
tion-makers, following the American model, have 
incorporated certain fundamental rights in Part III 
and made them immune from interference bv laws 
made by the State. We find it, however, difficult, in 
the absence of a clear indication to the contrary, to 
suppose that they also intended to make those rights 
immune from constitutional amendment. We are 
inclined to think that they must have had in mind 
what is of more frequent occurrence, that is, invasion 
of the rights of the subjects, by the legislative and the 
executive organs of the State by means of laws and 
rules made in exercise of their legislative power and 
not the abridgement or nullification of such rights by 
alterations of the Constitution itself in exercise. of 
sovereign constituent power. That power, though it 
has been entrusted to Parliament, has been so hedged 
about with restrictioru that its exercise must be diffi-
cult and rare. On the other hand, the terms of article 
368 are perfectly general and empower Parliament to 
amend the Constitution, without any exception what-
ever. Had it been intended to save the fundamental 
rights from the operation of that prov1s1on, it would 
have been perfectly easy to make that intention clear 
by adding a proviso to that effect. In short, we have 
here two articles each of which is widely phrased, but 
conflicts in its operation with the other. Harmonious 
construction requires that one should be read as con-
trolled and qualified by the other. Having regard to 
the considerations adverted to above, we are of opinion

The Constitution (First Amendment) 'Act, 1951, which has

The provisional Parliament is competent to exercise the power 
of amending the Constitution under Art. 368. The fact that the

the inference that the body which is invested with the power to

the two Houses. . 
The words "all the powers confer{ed by the provisions of this 
Constitution ori Parliament': in Art. 379 are not confined to such 
powers as could be exercised by · the provisional Parliament con-

Chapter IV of Part V and article 226 in Chapter V of

title: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala (1973) [Case Brief]
case_name: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala
facts: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act which restricted religious mutt property ownership, challenging the constitutional validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments under Article 368.
issues: What is the extent of Parliament's amending power under Article 368?
Can Parliament abrogate or alter the fundamental structure of the Constitution?
ratio_decidendi: Parliament has wide constituent amending power under Article 368 but cannot alter the 'Basic Structure' or essential features of the Indian Constitution. The Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.
verdict: Upheld 24th Amendment; partially struck down Article 31C; established the landmark Basic Structure Doctrine.

COURT: Supreme Court of India | BENCH: 13-Judge Bench (7:6 Majority)

STATUTES REFERRED: Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, 24th Amendment Act, 25th Amendment Act, 29th Amendment Act
FACTS & PROCEDURAL HISTORY: His Holiness Kesavananda Bharati challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act which restricted religious mutt property ownership, challenging the constitutional validity of the 24th, 25th, and 29th Amendments under Article 368.
ISSUES / QUESTIONS OF LAW: ["What is the extent of Parliament's amending power under Article 368?", 'Can Parliament abrogate or alter the fundamental structure of the Constitution?']
RATIO DECIDENDI: Parliament has wide constituent amending power under Article 368 but cannot alter the 'Basic Structure' or essential features of the Indian Constitution. The Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.
VERDICT & DISPOSITION: Upheld 24th Amendment; partially struck down Article 31C; established the landmark Basic Structure Doctrine.

title: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) [Case Brief]
case_name: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
facts: Allahabad High Court invalidated Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's election for corrupt electoral practices. Parliament enacted the 39th Amendment inserting Article 329A(4) placing election of PM and Speaker beyond judicial review.
issues: Does Article 329A(4) violate the Basic Structure of the Constitution?
ratio_decidendi: First direct application of Basic Structure Doctrine. Democracy, rule of law, equality (Article 14), and judicial review are basic features. A constitutional amendment placing an individual's election beyond judicial scrutiny violates the Basic Structure.

title: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) [Case Brief]
case_name: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India
facts: Minerva Mills challenged nationalization and the 42nd Amendment which added clauses (4) and (5) to Article 368 asserting unlimited amending power and expanded Article 31C to subordinate Fundamental Rights to all Directive Principles.
issues: Can Parliament grant itself unlimited amending power under Article 368?
Can Directive Principles take blanket precedence over Fundamental Rights?
ratio_decidendi: Limited amending power is itself a Basic Feature of the Constitution; Parliament cannot convert limited power into unlimited power. The harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is an essential basic feature.

title: I.R. Coelho (Dead) By LRs v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) [Case Brief]
case_name: I.R. Coelho (Dead) By LRs v. State of Tamil Nadu
facts: Referred to 9-judge bench to definitively resolve whether statutes placed in the Ninth Schedule after Kesavananda Bharati are completely immunized from judicial review for violating Fundamental Rights.
issues: Can Parliament insulate statutes violating Fundamental Rights from judicial review by putting them in Ninth Schedule?
ratio_decidendi: All laws placed in Ninth Schedule post-April 24, 1973 are subject to judicial review using the 'Rights Test' and 'Essence of Rights Test'. If a Ninth Schedule statute violates the principles underlying Articles 14, 19, or 21, it damages the Basic Structure and will be void.
verdict: Unanimously affirmed that Ninth Schedule cannot be used as a constitutional black hole to bypass the Basic Structure.

title: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) [Case Brief]
case_name: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
facts: Communist leader A.K. Gopalan was detained under Preventive Detention Act without trial. He claimed detention infringed freedom of movement under Article 19(1)(d) and personal liberty under Article 21.
issues: Does 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 incorporate American 'due process'?

title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) [Case Brief]
case_name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
facts: Regional Passport Office impounded Maneka Gandhi's passport 'in public interest' without furnishing reasons or providing a hearing.
issues: Is the right to travel abroad part of personal liberty under Article 21?

ratio_decidendi: Overruled Gopalan's silo approach; established the 'Golden Triangle' of Articles 14, 19, and 21. Any procedure depriving life or personal liberty must be 'just, fair, and reasonable' and not arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive. Right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty.

title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) [Case Brief]

facts: PIL petition letter by Executive Chairman, Legal Aid Services West Bengal, drawing attention to frequent custodial deaths and police brutality.

title: Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) [Case Brief]
case_name: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
facts: Appellants challenged involuntary administration of neuro-scientific investigative techniques: Narco-analysis (sodium pentothal), Polygraph test (lie detector), and Brain Electrical Activation Profile (BEAP).
issues: Does involuntary narco-analysis violate self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and mental privacy under Article 21?
ratio_decidendi: Involuntary administration of narco-analysis, polygraphy, and brain mapping constitutes testimonial compulsion violating Article 20(3) and infringes personal liberty and mental privacy under Article 21. Tests can only be administered voluntarily with informed consent.

title: Aruna Ramchandra Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011) [Case Brief]
case_name: Aruna Ramchandra Shanbaug v. Union of India
facts: Aruna Shanbaug, a nurse at KEM Hospital Mumbai, remained in a permanent vegetative state (PVS) for 37 years following a brutal sexual assault. Journalist Pinki Virani filed a writ petition seeking withdrawal of life support.
issues: Does Article 21 encompass the right to die with dignity?
Is passive euthanasia permissible under Indian constitutional law?
ratio_decidendi: Differentiated active euthanasia (administering lethal injection, prohibited) from passive euthanasia (withholding artificial life-support). Legalized passive euthanasia subject to strict High Court approval and medical board evaluation under the parens patriae doctrine.
verdict: Permitted passive euthanasia under judicial supervision; declined withdrawal for Aruna as KEM staff wished to care for her.

title: Common Cause (A Regd. Society) v. Union of India (2018) [Case Brief]
case_name: Common Cause (A Regd. Society) v. Union of India
facts: Common Cause filed PIL seeking legal recognition of 'living wills' (advance medical directives) enabling terminally ill patients to refuse artificial life prolongation.
issues: Is the right to die with dignity part of Article 21?

ratio_decidendi: Right to die with dignity is an inseparable facet of the fundamental right to live with dignity under Article 21. An adult person of sound mind has bodily autonomy to execute an Advance Medical Directive refusing artificial life support when death is imminent.

title: Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1963) [Case Brief]
case_name: Kharak Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh
facts: Kharak Singh, acquitted in a dacoity case, was subjected to police surveillance: secret picketing, domiciliary night visits, and verification of movements under U.P. Police Regulations.
issues: Does police surveillance and domiciliary night visits violate fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(d) and 21?

title: R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu (Auto Shankar Case) (1994) [Case Brief]
case_name: R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu (Auto Shankar Case)
facts: Condemned prisoner Auto Shankar wrote an autobiography disclosing unholy nexus with high-ranking police and prison officials. Prison authorities threatened publisher Nakkheeran with legal action to suppress publication.
issues: Does freedom of press include right to publish without pre-censorship?
What is the relationship between freedom of speech and citizen's right to privacy?
ratio_decidendi: Right to privacy is implicit in Article 21 ('right to be let alone'). A citizen has a right to safeguard the privacy of his family, marriage, procreation, and education. Public officials cannot suppress publication or claim damages for defamation unless statements are made with reckless disregard for truth.
verdict: Permitted publication; established tort of invasion of privacy and American New York Times v. Sullivan public official standard in India.

facts: Retired High Court Judge K.S. Puttaswamy challenged the mandatory Aadhaar biometric identification program. The Attorney General argued that under M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1963), the Constitution guaranteed no fundamental right to privacy.

title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Aadhaar Validity) (2018) [Case Brief]
case_name: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Aadhaar Validity)
acts_referred: Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016
facts: Substantive challenge to the constitutional validity of the Aadhaar Act, 2016, its passage as a Money Bill under Article 110, and mandatory linkage of Aadhaar to bank accounts, mobile SIM cards, school admissions, and welfare subsidies.
issues: Is the Aadhaar Act constitutionally valid under the Puttaswamy privacy proportionality test?
Was the Aadhaar Act legitimately passed as a Money Bill?
ratio_decidendi: Upheld core biometric Aadhaar for government welfare subsidies under Section 7 (legitimate state aim of preventing leakage). Upheld passage as Money Bill (Justice Chandrachud dissented).
verdict: Partially upheld Aadhaar for welfare subsidies; prohibited private corporate exploitation of Aadhaar database.

title: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) [Case Brief]
case_name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
facts: Two girls were arrested in Maharashtra under Section 66A of the IT Act for posting comments on Facebook questioning the city shutdown for Bal Thackeray's funeral. Law student Shreya Singhal filed a PIL challenging Section 66A.
issues: Does Section 66A IT Act violate freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a)?
Is Section 66A unconstitutionally vague and overbroad?
ratio_decidendi: Section 66A created a chilling effect on free online speech. Differentiated between discussion, advocacy, and incitement. A speech becomes restriction-worthy under Article 19(2) only when it reaches the level of incitement. The terms 'grossly offensive' and 'annoying' were hopelessly vague. Read down Section 79 intermediary guidelines to require court orders or government notifications for takedowns.
verdict: Struck down Section 66A IT Act in its entirety as unconstitutional; protected internet freedom in India.

title: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) [Case Brief]
case_name: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
facts: Following the revocation of Article 370 in August 2019, the government imposed indefinite internet shutdown and movement restrictions under Section 144 CrPC across Jammu and Kashmir. Editor of Kashmir Times challenged the blackout.
issues: Is access to the internet a fundamental right under Article 19?

ratio_decidendi: Freedom of speech and expression (Article 19(1)(a)) and freedom to carry on trade/business (Article 19(1)(g)) using the medium of the internet are constitutionally protected fundamental rights. title: State of Madras v. Srimathi Champakam Dorairajan (1951) [Case Brief]
case_name: State of Madras v. Srimathi Champakam Dorairajan
facts: Madras Government issued a Communal G.O. allocating medical and engineering college seats based strictly on caste and religious quotas. Brahmin student Champakam Dorairajan challenged the order after denial of admission.
issues: Does the Communal G.O. violate Article 15(1) and Article 29(2)?

title: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) [Case Brief]

facts: Senior IAS officer E.P. Royappa was transferred from the post of Chief Secretary to a newly created non-cadre post, which he challenged as arbitrary, malicious, and violative of Articles 14 and 16.
issues: What is the conceptual scope of equality under Article 14?
Does Article 14 strike down arbitrary state action?
ratio_decidendi: Formulated the revolutionary 'New Doctrine of Equality'. Equality is a dynamic concept with many aspects and dimensions and cannot be cribbed, cabined, and confined within traditional doctrinaire limits. Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies. title: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (Mandal Commission Case) (1992) [Case Brief]
case_name: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (Mandal Commission Case)
facts: V.P. Singh government implemented the Mandal Commission report reserving 27% vacancies in central civil services for Other Backward Classes (OBCs). Petitioners challenged the policy.
issues: Is caste alone a valid criterion for identifying backward classes?
What is the maximum permissible reservation ceiling?
Does reservation extend to promotions?
ratio_decidendi: Upheld 27% reservation for OBCs under Article 16(4). Caste can be an acceptable starting point for identifying backwardness. Established the 'Creamy Layer' exclusion principle for advanced sections of OBCs. Imposed a strict 50% ceiling on total reservations. Stated reservation applies only to initial appointments and not to promotions.
verdict: Upheld OBC reservation with creamy layer exclusion and 50% cap; prohibited reservation in promotions.

title: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006) [Case Brief]
case_name: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India
facts: Petitioners challenged the constitutional amendments that inserted Articles 16(4A) and 16(4B) providing reservation in promotions with consequential seniority for SCs and STs, overriding Indra Sawhney.
issues: Are constitutional amendments enabling reservation in promotion with consequential seniority valid?
ratio_decidendi: Upheld the constitutional validity of Articles 16(4A) and 16(4B). However, established three mandatory preconditions that the State must satisfy before granting reservations in promotion: (1) quantifiable data on backwardness, (2) inadequate representation in the specific service, and (3) overall administrative efficiency under Article 335.
verdict: Upheld 77th, 81st, 82nd, 85th Amendments subject to quantifiable data and efficiency requirements.

title: Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) [Case Brief]
case_name: Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta
acts_referred: M. Nagaraj v. Union of India (2006)
facts: Central Government sought reconsideration of M. Nagaraj (2006) by a 7-judge bench, arguing that requiring quantifiable data of backwardness for SCs and STs contradicted the presidential lists under Articles 341 and 342.
issues: Must the State collect quantifiable data showing backwardness for SC/ST promotions?
Does the Creamy Layer doctrine apply to SC/ST reservations in promotions?
ratio_decidendi: Modified Nagaraj: State does NOT need to collect quantifiable data on backwardness for SC/STs since their backwardness is presumed. However, affirmed that the 'Creamy Layer' doctrine applies to SCs and STs to prevent benefits from being cornered by elite sections.
verdict: Clarified that SC/ST backwardness is presumed; applied creamy layer principle to SC/ST promotions.

title: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (EWS Reservation Case) (2022) [Case Brief]
case_name: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (EWS Reservation Case)
facts: Challenge to the 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 which introduced 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) excluding existing SC, ST, and SEBC beneficiaries.
issues: Does reservation based solely on economic criteria violate the Basic Structure?
Does excluding SCs/STs/OBCs from EWS violate equality?
Does breaching the 50% ceiling violate the Basic Structure?
ratio_decidendi: Majority (Justices Maheshwari, Trivedi, Pardiwala) held that economic criteria is a valid basis for affirmative classification and does not violate the Basic Structure. verdict: Upheld the validity of the 103rd Amendment Act (10% EWS reservation) by 3:2 majority.

title: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950) [Case Brief]
case_name: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras
acts_referred: Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949
facts: Madras Government banned entry and circulation of Romesh Thappar's left-wing weekly journal 'Cross Roads' under public safety provisions.
issues: Does freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) include freedom of circulation?
Can public order justify bans when 'public order' was not in original Article 19(2)?
ratio_decidendi: Freedom of speech and expression includes freedom of propagation of ideas, which is ensured through freedom of circulation. There can be no freedom of speech without freedom of circulation. Restrictions outside the specific heads in Article 19(2) are void.
verdict: Struck down the circulation ban; led to First Amendment adding 'public order' to Article 19(2).

title: Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India (1973) [Case Brief]
case_name: Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India
facts: Government restricted import and quota of newsprint and imposed a 10-page ceiling on major daily newspapers (Times of India) under economic import regulations.
issues: Does newsprint quota and page-ceiling violate freedom of the press under Article 19(1)(a)?
ratio_decidendi: Direct effect and operational consequence test: Government cannot indirectly curtail freedom of the press under the guise of regulating newsprint commerce. Freedom of the press means freedom from commercial restrictions on pagination and circulation.

title: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (National Anthem Case) (1986) [Case Brief]
case_name: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (National Anthem Case)
acts_referred: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
facts: Three school children belonging to Jehovah's Witnesses stood respectfully when the National Anthem was sung in school assembly, but did not sing along due to conscientious religious tenets. They were expelled.
issues: Does expulsion for respectfully standing without singing the National Anthem violate Articles 19(1)(a) and 25(1)?
ratio_decidendi: Freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) includes the right to remain silent. Standing up respectfully shows proper reverence; no law obliges any citizen to sing. Expulsion violated religious freedom (Article 25) and speech (Article 19(1)(a)).
verdict: Quashed expulsion; held our tradition teaches tolerance, our philosophy preaches tolerance, our Constitution practices tolerance.

title: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985) [Case Brief]
case_name: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum
facts: 62-year-old divorced Muslim woman Shah Bano sought maintenance from her wealthy advocate husband under Section 125 CrPC. The husband argued Muslim personal law limited maintenance to the iddat period.
issues: Does Section 125 CrPC apply to divorced Muslim women notwithstanding personal law?
Is Section 125 secular in nature?
ratio_decidendi: Section 125 CrPC is a secular, compassionate statutory measure designed to prevent destitution and vagrancy. It applies to all citizens regardless of religion. It overrides personal laws where a divorced wife is unable to maintain herself. Highlighted the necessity of a Uniform Civil Code (Article 44).
verdict: Awarded maintenance to Shah Bano; affirmed secular primacy of Section 125 CrPC.

title: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (Triple Talaq Case) (2017) [Case Brief]
case_name: Shayara Bano v. Union of India (Triple Talaq Case)
facts: Shayara Bano challenged the practice of Talaq-e-Biddat (instantaneous, irrevocable Triple Talaq pronounced in a single sitting) as violative of equality, non-discrimination, and dignity.
issues: Is Talaq-e-Biddat an essential religious practice protected under Article 25?
Is instant triple talaq manifestly arbitrary under Article 14?
ratio_decidendi: Talaq-e-Biddat is not an essential religious practice in Islamic theology. Justice Nariman held that instant triple talaq allows marital breakdown at the capricious whims of the husband without reconciliation, making it 'manifestly arbitrary' and void under Article 14.
verdict: Struck down Triple Talaq by 3:2 majority as unconstitutional; established manifest arbitrariness doctrine.

title: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) [Case Brief]

acts_referred: Convention on Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW)
facts: Social worker Bhanwari Devi was gang-raped for attempting to stop child marriage in rural Rajasthan. Women's rights groups filed a PIL seeking workplace safety guidelines in the absence of enacted legislation.

facts: NALSA filed PIL seeking formal legal recognition for transgender individuals who were historically marginalized, denied civic rights, and forced into binary male/female categories.

title: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (Decriminalization of Section 377) (2018) [Case Brief]
case_name: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (Decriminalization of Section 377)
facts: LGBTQ+ activists challenged Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, which criminalized consensual sexual acts 'against the order of nature', following the retrograde reversal in Suresh Koushal (2013).
issues: Does criminalizing consensual adult same-sex intimacy violate Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21?
ratio_decidendi: Constitutional morality prevails over public/social morality. Consensual adult sexual intimacy in private is protected under privacy, personal autonomy, and dignity (Article 21). Discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited under Article 15(1) ('sex' includes sexual orientation).
verdict: Decriminalized consensual homosexual sex by reading down Section 377; recognized constitutional morality.

title: Joseph Shine v. Union of India (Decriminalization of Adultery) (2018) [Case Brief]
case_name: Joseph Shine v. Union of India (Decriminalization of Adultery)
facts: Non-resident Indian Joseph Shine filed PIL challenging Section 497 IPC which punished a man for adultery with a married woman without consent of her husband, treating the woman as chattel of her husband.
issues: Does Section 497 IPC treat women as property of men, violating Articles 14, 15, and 21?
ratio_decidendi: Section 497 IPC is based on archaic patriarchal stereotypes reducing women to the chattel of their husbands. It punishes the outsider man while treating the woman as an object without agency, violating Article 14 and Article 15. Matrimonial infidelity is a civil ground for divorce, not a criminal offence under state penal sanctions.
verdict: Unanimously struck down Section 497 IPC and Section 198(2) CrPC as unconstitutional.

title: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges Case) (1981) [Case Brief]
case_name: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges Case)
facts: Challenge to government circular on non-appointment of additional High Court judges and mass transfers of High Court judges without concurrence of Chief Justice of India.
issues: Does 'consultation' in Articles 124 and 217 mean 'concurrence' of the Chief Justice of India?
ratio_decidendi: 'Consultation' does not mean 'concurrence'. The executive holds primacy in judicial appointments and transfers, provided there is full and effective consultation. Also established expansive rules of locus standi for Public Interest Litigation (PIL).

title: In re Special Reference No. 1 of 1998 (Third Judges Case) (1998) [Case Brief]
case_name: In re Special Reference No. 1 of 1998 (Third Judges Case)
facts: President K.R. Narayanan sought an advisory opinion under Article 143 regarding the consultative process and collegium composition for appointing Supreme Court and High Court judges.
issues: What is the exact composition and quorum of the Collegium for judicial appointments and transfers?
ratio_decidendi: Expanded Collegium: For Supreme Court appointments, CJI must consult a collegium of 4 senior-most Supreme Court judges. For High Court appointments, CJI consults 2 senior-most judges. If majority of collegium advises against appointment, CJI shall not send recommendation.
verdict: Consolidated and institutionalized the 5-member Supreme Court Collegium framework.

title: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (NJAC Case / Fourth Judges) (2015) [Case Brief]
case_name: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (NJAC Case / Fourth Judges)
facts: Parliament unanimously enacted 99th Amendment and NJAC Act creating a 6-member Commission (CJI, 2 senior judges, Union Law Minister, and 2 eminent persons) with veto power to replace the Collegium.
issues: Does the inclusion of executive members in judicial selection infringe judicial independence as a Basic Feature?

title: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (Bihar Assembly Dissolution) (2006) [Case Brief]
case_name: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (Bihar Assembly Dissolution)
facts: Following inconclusive Bihar assembly elections in 2005, the Governor sent a midnight report claiming horse-trading, prompting the Union Cabinet to recommend dissolution of the newly elected assembly before its first meeting.
issues: Can an assembly be dissolved to prevent political parties from staking a claim?

title: State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to Governor of Punjab (2023) [Case Brief]
case_name: State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to Governor of Punjab
facts: Governor of Punjab refused to grant assent to multiple bills passed by the Vidhan Sabha, claiming the speaker's reconvening of the budget session was illegal and withholding assent indefinitely.
issues: Can a Governor withhold assent indefinitely under Article 200 without returning bills to the Assembly?
ratio_decidendi: Governors cannot sit indefinitely on bills passed by elected state legislatures. Under Article 200, if a Governor decides to withhold assent, he must return the bill to the legislature 'as soon as possible' for reconsideration. A Governor is a symbolic constitutional head and cannot veto democratic legislation.
verdict: Mandated that Governors act promptly; prohibited indefinite pocket-vetoes of state legislation.

title: In re Article 370 of the Constitution (2023) [Case Brief]
case_name: In re Article 370 of the Constitution
acts_referred: Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Orders C.O. 272 and C.O. 273
facts: Challenge to the abrogating Presidential Orders C.O. 272 and C.O. 273 of August 2019 which rendered Article 370 inoperative and bifurcated Jammu and Kashmir into two Union Territories.
issues: Was Article 370 permanent or temporary?
Could Article 370 be abrogated when J&K was under President's Rule?
ratio_decidendi: Article 370 was a temporary transitional provision intended to facilitate constitutional integration of Jammu and Kashmir into the Indian Union. Upon signing the Instrument of Accession, J&K retained no internal sovereignty. The President had the power to issue notifications declaring Article 370 inoperative.
verdict: Unanimously upheld the constitutional validity of abrogating Article 370; directed statehood restoration and elections by September 2024.

title: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) (1987) [Case Brief]
case_name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case)
facts: Severe leak of hazardous Oleum gas from Shriram Foods and Fertilizer plant in Delhi shortly after the Bhopal disaster, causing deaths and mass panic. M.C. Mehta filed PIL under Article 32.
issues: What is the standard of liability for hazardous and inherently dangerous industrial enterprises?
ratio_decidendi: Evolved the landmark 'Absolute Liability' doctrine, discarding the 19th-century English Rylands v. Fletcher strict liability with its exceptions. An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community. Compensation must be correlated to the magnitude and financial capacity of the enterprise.
verdict: Established Absolute Liability in Indian tort and constitutional jurisprudence.

title: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (Pavement Dwellers Case) (1985) [Case Brief]
case_name: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (Pavement Dwellers Case)
facts: BMC initiated eviction of pavement and slum dwellers from Bombay footpaths without notice or alternative rehabilitation during monsoon rains.
issues: Does the right to life under Article 21 include the right to livelihood?
ratio_decidendi: The right to livelihood is an integral facet of the right to life under Article 21. If the right to livelihood is not treated as part of the right to life, the easiest way of depriving a person of his life would be to deprive him of his means of livelihood. Eviction cannot be executed without notice and reasonable opportunity of being heard.

title: Unni Krishnan, J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) [Case Brief]

facts: Challenge to state schemes regulating exorbitant capitation fees charged by private unaided medical and engineering colleges.
issues: Is education a fundamental right under Article 21?

title: Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013) [Case Brief]

facts: Section 8(4) of the RPA protected sitting MPs and MLAs convicted of serious crimes from disqualification if they filed an appeal within three months.

title: Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (Electoral Bonds Case) (2024) [Case Brief]
case_name: Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (Electoral Bonds Case)
facts: Government introduced Electoral Bonds Scheme 2018 permitting anonymous, unlimited political contributions by corporations and individuals without public disclosure.
issues: Does unlimited anonymous political funding infringe voter's right to information under Article 19(1)(a)?
Does allowing loss-making corporations to donate violate Article 14?
ratio_decidendi: Voter's right to information regarding political party funding is essential for participatory electoral democracy under Article 19(1)(a). title: Sita Soren v. Union of India (Legislative Bribery Immunity Case) (2024) [Case Brief]
case_name: Sita Soren v. Union of India (Legislative Bribery Immunity Case)
facts: JMM MLA Sita Soren was accused of accepting a bribe to vote for an independent candidate in Rajya Sabha elections. She claimed constitutional immunity under Article 194(2) relying on P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).
issues: Does parliamentary privilege protect MPs/MLAs from criminal prosecution for accepting bribes to speak or vote?
ratio_decidendi: Parliamentary privilege under Articles 105(2) and 194(2) exists to foster deliberative democratic independence, not to confer exemption from ordinary criminal law. The crime of bribery is complete the moment the bribe is accepted, irrespective of whether the vote is subsequently cast.
verdict: Unanimously overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao; held legislators taking bribes enjoy no immunity from prosecution.
